text.p: After playing bridesmaid all season to teammate Thomas Sykora, Austria's Thomas Stangassinger took advantage of the World Cup slalom leader's misfortune to win a men's World Cup slalom on Sunday.
Stangassinger, second after the first run that claimed more than a third of the 62 starters including Sykora, posted the fastest second-leg time for a combined time of one minute, 41.10 seconds.
Only 24 of 30 starters completed the second run down the icy pitch where Olympic slalom events will be held at next year's Nagano Olympics.
"It wasn't a perfect race, but the conditions were very difficult today," said Stangassinger.

The win, his first in three years and fifth of his career, kept alive the 31-year-old veteran's hopes of overtaking Sykora for the slalom title, which will be decided next week at the World Cup finals in Vail, Colorado.

Two Norwegians finished behind Stangassinger, gold medallist at the 1994 Lillehammer Olympics. Finn Christian Jagge was second in 1:41.94, while Ole Christian Furuseth took third in 1:42.32 for his first podium appearance this season.

Furuseth, the last skier down the 607-metre Mount Yakebitai course, narrowly edged crowd favourite Kiminobu Kimura of Japan out of the medals after officials checked video replays to ensure Furuseth had not missed a gate in the middle section.
Even Furuseth had thought his momentary loss of balance spelled disaster.
"I thought I was out of the race, so I just tried to get down fast," he said. "If I hadn't made that mistake, I think I could have challenged Thomas."
Kimuras's fourth-place finish was Japan's best World Cup result since Tetsuya Okabe placed second in a men's slalom nine years ago.
Stangassinger, who finished second to Sykora in three World Cup races this season, needs to win or place second at Vail to overtake Sykora, who leads the slalom standings with 666 points.
Stangassinger has 590 points while Sebastien Amiez of France, fifth on Saturday, trails with 373 points.
Fourth-ranked Alberto Tomba also did not survive the first run after his skis crossed mid-way down the course.
"It is too early in the morning for me," said the Italian star. "I'm sorry for the people who came to watch me."
Norwegian Kjetil Andre Aamodt, who is chasing Luc Alphand for the World Cup overall lead, finished 10th to edge closer to the French speed specialist. Aamodt now trails Alphand by 117 points.
Stangassiner and Furuseth both approved of Mount Yakebitai as an Olympic course, although Jagge thought it was not challenging enough.
"I dont think it is too easy," said Stangassinger. "I think it's much nice than Sestriere, not too steep and not too flat."
Furuseth said the mountain would produce a fairer race than the Wengen or Kitzbuehel courses.
